L0@P0: GLOBAL MIGRATION AND REGIONALIZATION, 1840-1940
L1@P0: Paper for conference on Mapping Global Inequalities
L2@P0: Santa Cruz, California
L3@P0: December 13-14, 2007
L4@P0: Adam McKeown
L5@P0: Associate Professor of History
L6@P0: Columbia University
L7@P0: amm2009@columbia.edu
L8@P0: The mass migrations of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries were a global
L9@P0: phenomenon. From the North Atlantic to the South Pacific, hardly any corner of the earth
L10@P0: was untouched by migration. These migrations similar in quantity and organization, and
L11@P0: all linked through the processes of globalization: the peopling of frontiers, new
L12@P0: transportation technologies, the production and processing of material for modern
L13@P0: industry, the shipment and marketing of finished goods, and the production of food,
L14@P0: shelter and clothing for people who worked in those industrial and distribution networks.
L15@P0: It was a truly global process. Yet, the processes and cycles of migration grew
L16@P0: increasingly integrated across the globe, the actual patterns and directions of migration
L17@P0-1: grew more regionally segregated. These segregated regions experienced different patterns2
L18@P1: of development and growth associated with migration. Moreover, this segregation helped
L19@P1: to erase many of the non-Atlantic migrations from the historical memory, thus helping to
L20@P1: obscure inequalities that were created as part of historical globalization by depicting
L21@P1: certain parts of the world as having been outside of globalization.
L22@P1: Most histories have recounted the age of mass migration as a transatlantic age.
L23@P1: When migrations beyond the Atlantic are remembered at all, it is usually as a limited
L24@P1: number of indentured laborers pressed into the service of Europeans. This historical
L25@P1: memory is not random. It is the foundation of the broadest of global identities: East and
L26@P1: West, North and South, First and Third Worlds, and the liberal and illiberal regions of the
L27@P1: modern international system. It corresponds with depictions of European migrants as
L28@P1: pioneering settlers who opened frontiers and constructed new nations, bearing individual
L29@P1: initiative and progress to the cutting edge of world history. Asians, in contrast, are
L30@P1: remembered as backwards and earth-bound peasants unable to participate in the sweep of
L31@P1: modern history except as impoverished sojourners compelled by external dynamism and
L32@P1: coercive intervention.1
L33@P1: In fact, Asian migrations were as numerous as the Atlantic migrations, and
L34@P1: organized through similar networks. In the middle of the nineteenth century, trends of
L35@P1: Asian migration to the Americas and Australasia had the potential to create densely
L36@P1: integrated patterns of global migration that linked the eastern and western hemispheres.
L37@P1: By the end of the century, however, Asian migration was largely cut off from the
L38@P1: Americas and white settler colonies. State interventions and redirected shipping routes
L39@P1: had divided global migration into distinct regional systems by establishing barriers across
L40@P1-2: the Pacific Ocean and Eastern Mediterranean. The great publicity surrounding indenture,3
L41@P2: and increasingly racialized stereotypes about a backwards Asia helped entrench a
L42@P2: narrative of globalization as a dynamic center that expands to engulf the world rather than
L43@P2: divide and segregate it. The isolation of the rest of the world is seen as a natural
L44@P2: consequence of distance and cultural differences rather that the product of interaction and
L45@P2: state intervention. In fact, however, the segmentation of the world into unequal regions
L46@P2: has been an inseparable from the processes of integration.
L47@P2: Memories of Migration
L48@P2: It is easy to find assertions in state of the field volumes on migration history that
L49@P2: privilege the uniqueness of the transatlantic system. Many of these are simply statements
L50@P2: of quantity, such as the assertion that “By chance or choice, almost half of these worldtravelers settled in the United States.”2 Some go further and assert that transatlantic
L51@P2: migration was also different in quality, such as the claim that,
L52@P2: It is North and South America in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries that
L53@P2: provide the great stage for the migration drama, where migration assumes
L54@P2: extraordinary dimensions. While for the other continents migration was a means
L55@P2: of relieving demographic pressure by moving surplus population to regions of
L56@P2: lower density, in North and South America the problem was one of providing a
L57@P2: labor force to work the vast areas of open land waiting to be brought under
L58@P2-3: cultivation.34
L59@P3: Other statements of transatlantic uniqueness are intended to highlight the increasingly
L60@P3: global quality of contemporary migration, such as the assertion that “Although
L61@P3: international migrants were not exclusively European, the overwhelming majority came
L62@P3: from that continent. . . . Before 1925, 85 percent of all international migrants originated
L63@P3: in Europe, but since 1960 Europe has contributed an increasingly small fraction of
L64@P3: emigrants to world migration flows.”4 In The Age of Mass Migration, Hatton and
L65@P3: Williamson justify their exclusive focus on the North Atlantic with an argument that the
L66@P3: inherent qualities of the “present Third World” led to its isolation from the historical
L67@P3: processes of globalization until recently. These regions “were segmented by
L68@P3: discrimination, language, and custom. They were segmented by long distance and high
L69@P3: migration cost. They were segmented by the poverty of the Third World labor-surplus
L70@P3: areas, areas so poor that potential emigrants would have found it impossible to finance
L71@P3: the move to the booming OECD labor markets anyway.”5 By placing migrations beyond
L72@P3: the Atlantic outside of globalization their argument that globalization leads to economic
L73@P3: convergence becomes a tautology: globalization causes economic convergence because
L74@P3: only places that converged are considered to be sites of globalization.
L75@P3: These citations could be dismissed as grounded in a lack of information. But the
L76@P3: entrenchment of these assumptions only perpetuates this lack of knowledge, and few of
L77@P3: these volumes give much attention to areas beyond the Atlantic except in ways that
L78@P3: confirm those basic assumptions, down to the very frameworks for collecting data. This
L79@P3: can be seen in Pieter Emmer’s comparative work which categorizes long distance
L80@P3: migration as being intercontinental or not. He includes Russians who crossed the Ural
L81@P3-4: Mountains and French to Algeria as intercontinental, but not Chinese to Singapore or5
L82@P4: Hadhrami to Java. After counting 5 to 6 million intercontinental African and Asian
L83@P4: migrants from 1800 to 1960, he concludes that “The study of migration as part of the
L84@P4: process of European expansion and contraction clearly shows that Europeans have
L85@P4: participated much more extensively in intercontinental migrations than Africans and
L86@P4: Asians.”6 This distinction then becomes the basis for qualitative judgments. In his essay,
L87@P4: “Was Migration Beneficial?” he divides global migration into temperate and tropical
L88@P4: plantation systems, the latter made up almost entirely of indentured Asians and Africans.
L89@P4: He then suggests that it does not make much sense to ask if Asian migration was
L90@P4: beneficial “given the relatively small volume of both internal and external migration,”
L91@P4: thus dismissing the relevance of much of the world in understanding global processes.
L92@P4: 7
L93@P4: Emmer’s distinctions may seem crude, but the general assumption that Asians did
L94@P4: not migrate and that those who did consisted almost entirely of indentured labor
L95@P4: dominated by Europeans pervades much of the literature.This assumption is somewhat
L96@P4: understandable for Indian migration given its relatively tight organization within the
L97@P4: British Empire and the relatively high level of assisted migration to European owned
L98@P4: plantations. Much more perplexing is the characterization of Chinese overseas migration
L99@P4: as indentured and the consistently low estimations of Chinese migration in Western
L100@P4: language scholarship, ranging from 2 to 8 million (which, as we shall see, accounts for
L101@P4: less than half of all Chinese emigration).
L102@P4: 8 Most of these numbers were ultimately drawn
L103@P4: from three studies by Chen Ta, Chen Zexuan and Arnold Meagher, all of which were
L104@P4: counting only contract labor migration.
L105@P4: 9 But even the incomplete Chinese numbers in
L106@P4: Ferenczi and Willcox’s International Migrations, still the most widely used source of
L107@P4-5: migration statistics, count 5.5 million immigrants to the Straits Settlements from 1881 to 6
L108@P5: 1915, 3.7 million departing Chinese ports from 1876 to 1901, and 2.4 million leaving
L109@P5: Hong Kong from 1900-1924. This already accounts for up to 8 million Chinese within a
L110@P5: limited period, not including the indentures (mostly before 1874) that make up other
L111@P5: estimates.
L112@P5: 10 Extrapolation from these numbers could easily have provided a much larger
L113@P5: figure for Chinese migration, if not for assumptions that Chinese did not migrate.
L114@P5: One recent history of global migration explains the causes of Chinese migration
L115@P5: overseas and to Manchuria as, “Imperial Chinese maladministration and revolts,
L116@P5: overpopulation and natural disasters as well as colonial penetration.”
L117@P5: 11 Research on
L118@P5: European migrations (as the author demonstrates elsewhere) has consistently argued that
L119@P5: the first three causes rarely, if ever, explain the establishment of steady migration patterns
L120@P5: from Europe. And “colonial penetration” is, of course, irrelevant for Europe. This
L121@P5: explanation leaves the impression that Chinese did not migrate according to the same
L122@P5: kinds of processes that produced European migration. Without European intervention,
L123@P5: Asians would have remained tradition-bound, immobile peasants, subject only to Asian
L124@P5: despotisms and crude Malthusian pressures. In other words, the overall effect is to render
L125@P5: them categorically different from the trans-Atlantic migrations that were a crucible of the
L126@P5: modern world.
L127@P5: Forgetting also happens in other parts of the world. For example, Chinese scholars
L128@P5: generally consider the Manchurian migrations to be a form of domestic movement that is
L129@P5: irrelevant to global comparison.12 But the current Manchurian population of over 100
L130@P5: million suggests a demographic transition similar to those of European settler colonies in
L131@P5: the Americas. Without these migrations, Manchuria might not be a part of China today,
L132@P5-6: but part of Russia, Japan, or an independent nation like Mongolia. National borders have7
L133@P6: reinforced the understandings of world migration framed by the division of the world into
L134@P6: macroregions.
L135@P6: Long Distance Migration
L136@P6: Rather than start with assumptions about the distinctness of different systems, let
L137@P6: us start with migration data. Port and customs statistics from around the world support an
L138@P6: estimate of at least 150 million long distance voyages from 1840 to 1940, spread over
L139@P6: much of the world (table 1).
L140@P6: 13 This number mostly counts ship passengers who traveled in
L141@P6: third class or steerage, people categorized as “immigrants”, “emigrants” or “laborers,”
L142@P6: and migrants who registered under officially sponsored colonization schemes like those
L143@P6: from Russia to Siberia and Central Asia. Data for return voyages is less readily available,
L144@P6: so (as with most migration statistics) this estimate includes multiple trips by single
L145@P6: individuals. It does not count people who traveled overland or in first class, or the other
L146@P6: migrants who avoided inspection and enumeration. The prevalence of these evasions is
L147@P6: apparent in comparing numbers from emigration and immigration ports that sometimes
L148@P6: vary by 20 percent or more.
L149@P6: 14 Thus, estimates like this can only describe general trends
L150@P6: but are still useful as a basis for broad comparisons.

L175@P7: The bulk of these long distance migrations can be classified according to three
L176@P7: systems that were similar in quantity and connected major sending and receiving regions:
L177@P7: transatlantic migration from Europe to the Americas; from India and South China to a
L178@P7: region centered on Southeast Asia but extending across the rims of the Indian Ocean and
L179@P7: the South Pacific; and from Russia, north China and Korea into the broad expanse of
L180@P7: North Asia stretching from the Russian steppes to Siberia and Manchuria. The three
L181@P7-8: destinations were the great frontier settlement regions of the modern world. Smaller9
L182@P8: auxiliary flows moved across these systems, but accounted for less than five percent of
L183@P8: the total movement.
L184@P8: Transatlantic. The migration of Europeans to the Americas is the best known of
L185@P8: these migrations. Nearly 65 percent went to the United States, with the bulk of the
L186@P8: remainder divided between Argentina (which had the largest proportion of foreign born
L187@P8: residents), Canada, Brazil and, to a lesser extent, Cuba and Uruguay.15 Over half of the
L188@P8: emigration before the 1870s was from the British Isles, with much of the remainder from
L189@P8: Northwest Europe. As migration increased along with new transportation technologies in
L190@P8: the 1880s, regions of intensive emigration spread south and east as far as Portugal,
L191@P8: Russia, and Syria. Up to 2.5 million migrants from South and East Asia also traveled to
L192@P8: the Americas, mostly to the frontiers of western North America or the plantations of the
L193@P8: Caribbean, Peru and Brazil. Half of the Asian migration took place from 1850 to 1885,
L194@P8: after which the decline of indentured labor recruitment and the rise of anti-Asian
L195@P8: immigration laws took effect.
L196@P8: Southeast Asia-Indian Ocean. Migration to Southeast Asia and lands around the
L197@P8: Indian Ocean and South Pacific consisted of over 29 million Indians, at least 19 million
L198@P8: Chinese, and about 4.5 million Europeans, mostly to Australia, New Zealand and South
L199@P8: Africa. Most migration from India was to colonies throughout the British Empire. Nearly
L200@P8: 4 million Indians traveled to Malaysia, over 8 million to Ceylon, over 15 million to
L201@P8: Burma, and about a million to Africa, other parts of Southeast Asia and islands
L202@P8: throughout the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Despite the notoriety and extensive debates
L203@P8: over Indian indenture, less than 8 percent of total migration from India was indentured at
L204@P8-9: the time of departure, mostly to distant places in the Americas, Africa and Fiji. The10
L205@P9: proportion declined over time, accounting for about a quarter of Indian emigration from
L206@P9: 1840 to 1860 and quickly decreasing to an average of 5 percent a year until imposition of
L207@P9: restrictions on indenture contracts after 1908 and the abolishment of indenture in 1920
L208@P9: brought it down to nothing. A majority of Indian migration to Southeast Asia was still
L209@P9: undertaken with under some form of assistance or debt obligation through native kangani
L210@P9: and maistry labor recruitment systems. Up to two million migrated as merchants or
L211@P9: travelers not intending to work as laborers.
L212@P9: 16
L213@P9: The vast majority of Chinese migrants came from the southern provinces of
L214@P9: Guangdong and Fujian. Up to 11 million traveled from China to Singapore and Penang,
L215@P9: from where more than a third of these transshipped to the Dutch Indies, Borneo, Burma
L216@P9: and places further west. Nearly 4 million traveled directly from China to Thailand,
L217@P9: between 2 and 3 million to French Indochina, over a million directly to the Dutch Indies
L218@P9: (for a total of over 4 million if transshipments from Singapore are included), less than a
L219@P9: million to the Philippines, and about half a million to Australia, New Zealand, Hawaii
L220@P9: and other islands in the Pacific and Indian Oceans.
L221@P9: 17 Given the wide variety of labor
L222@P9: recruitment and financing schemes and the fact that many migrants were trained to tell
L223@P9: inspectors that they had not signed a contract, it is difficult to determine the number of
L224@P9: migrants who migrated with labor contracts. Less than three quarters of a million Chinese
L225@P9: migrants signed indenture contracts with European employers, including a quarter million
L226@P9: to Latin America and the Caribbean before 1874, a quarter million to Sumatra from the
L227@P9: 1880s to the 1910s, and a smaller number to mines, plantations and islands scattered
L228@P9: throughout Malaya and the Pacific and Indian Oceans. From 1881 to 1913, 776,457 labor
L229@P9-10: contracts (about 12 percent of all immigrants) were signed in front of the Protector of11
L230@P10: Chinese in Singapore by migrants who had not paid their own passage. These ranged
L231@P10: from indentures to Chinese and European planters in Malaya and Sumatra to agreements
L232@P10: for cooperative profit sharing in Malayan tin mines.
L233@P10: 18 Many, if not most Chinese paid for
L234@P10: their own passage or borrowed money from relatives and friends. Others had their
L235@P10: original passage paid by wealthy Chinese under the “credit-ticket” system, although the
L236@P10: terms of repayment varied and the migrants were not necessarily bound to work for their
L237@P10: creditors. In all cases, the organization of migration was largely independent of European
L238@P10: regulation, but deeply linked to the expansion of a Europe-centered global economy.
L239@P10: Northern Asia. Migrants had trickled into Central Asia, Siberia and Manchuria for
L240@P10: hundreds of years before the Qing government’s gradual relaxation of restrictions against
L241@P10: movement into Manchuria after the 1850s and the emancipation of serfs and opening of
L242@P10: Siberia by Russia in 1861. Both governments actively encouraged settlement with
L243@P10: homesteading policies in the 1880s, each attempting to counter territorial encroachment
L244@P10: by the other. Railroad construction in the 1890s further strengthened the migrant flows.
L245@P10: At least 13 million Russians moved into Central Asia and Siberia. This briefly reversed in
L246@P10: the 1920s as local policies were erected against Russian settlers, but resumed familiar
L247@P10: eastward patterns by the mid-1920s when central directives overrode local policies.
L248@P10: 19
L249@P10: Between 28 and 33 million Chinese migrated into Manchuria and Siberia, along with
L250@P10: nearly 2 million Koreans. Another two and a half million Koreans migrated to Japan,
L251@P10: especially in the 1930s, and over two million Japanese also moved in to Korea and
L252@P10: Manchuria. In addition, up to a million north Chinese, Koreans and Japanese migrated to
L253@P10: a diverse range of destinations, including much of the Americas, Hawaii, Southeast Asia,
L254@P10: South Africa and Europe.
L255@P10-11: 2012
L256@P11: These migrations caused a significant redistribution of the world’s population. All
L257@P11: three destination regions experienced massive population growth, with their populations
L258@P11: increasing by factors of 4 to 5.5 from 1850 to 1950 (table 2 and figure A). Growth rates
L259@P11: in these areas were over twice that for world population as a whole. In comparison,
L260@P11: growth rates in the sending regions were lower than world population growth and less
L261@P11: than half of those in the receiving regions. Taken together, the three main destination
L262@P11: regions accounted for 10 percent of the world’s population in 1850 and 24 percent in
L263@P11: 1950. The Americas and northern Asia grew more quickly than Southeast Asia with its
L264@P11: smaller area, tropical environment and more entrenched native population. Nonetheless,
L265@P11: from 1870 to 1930 approximately 35 million migrants moved into the 4.1 million square
L266@P11: kilometers of Southeast Asia, compared to the 39 million migrants that moved into the
L267@P11: 9.8 million square kilometers of the United States.

L289@P12: Emigration was uneven from specific localities within broader regions. Some
L290@P12: villages or counties sent numerous migrants while others sent hardly any at all. But
L291@P12: average emigration rates from the sending regions are broadly comparable. At first glance
L292@P12: 19 million overseas emigrants from China or 29 million from India seems like a drop in
L293@P12: the bucket compared to the several millions from much smaller countries like Italy,
L294@P12: Norway, Ireland and England.21 But if we adjust the focus to regions of comparable size
L295@P12: and population, the rates are very similar. Some peak rates of overseas emigration from
L296@P12: Europe in the 1910s are 10.8 emigrants per 1,000 population in Italy, 8.3 from Norway,
L297@P12: and 7 from Ireland.22 In comparison, the annual average overseas emigration rate from
L298@P12: Guangdong province in south China, which had a slightly larger geographic area and
L299@P12: slightly smaller population than Italy, was at least 9.6 per 1,000 in the peak years of the
L300@P12-13: 1920s. Hebei and Shandong provinces (sources of migration to Manchuria) had an even 14
L301@P13: higher rate of 10 during that same decade.
L302@P13: 23 In terms of broader regional population,
L303@P13: emigration from Europe from 1846 to 1940 amounted to 15.4 percent of the European
L304@P13: population in 1900, compared to 11.3 in China and 10.4 in South Asia. This latter
L305@P13: difference is not insignificant (and only tentative, given our lack of knowledge of internal
L306@P13: and overland migration), but certainly does not justify a categorical distinction between
L307@P13: quantity and quality of migration in the different regions.
L308@P13: Other Migrations
L309@P13: Trans-oceanic migration within these three systems was only the tip of the iceberg
L310@P13: of global migration. Other migration moved in and out of places such as Africa and the
L311@P13: Middle East that were at the interstices of the main long-distance systems. Overland and
L312@P13: domestic migration, much of it within the main sending and receiving regions, also
L313@P13: generally escaped the web of enumerators and inspectors. Perhaps the great majority of
L314@P13: global migration was seasonal, temporary and permanent movement to nearby cities,
L315@P13: towns, factories, mines, agricultural regions and unused lands.
L316@P13: The transatlantic migrations could be extended to include over 13 million people
L317@P13: who moved to the Western frontiers of North America, first primarily across the United
L318@P13: States and then into the western plains of Canada. This process also included the
L319@P13: relocation of great numbers of Native Americans and the migration of over 2.5 million
L320@P13: Mexicans to the agricultural areas of the southwest in the early twentieth century. The
L321@P13: industrial centers of the northeastern United States also attracted over 2.5 million
L322@P13: Canadians, and then over a million African Americans and Mexicans in the early
L323@P13-14: twentieth century.24 In other parts of the Americas, great numbers of Andean and other15
L324@P14: peoples moved to coastal plantations and cities, and over 300,000 Caribbean peoples
L325@P14: migrated to plantations in Central America and Cuba, to the Panama Canal Zone, and the
L326@P14: United States.
L327@P14: 25 Migrants also moved within Southeast Asia and the South Pacific. These
L328@P14: included up to 500,000 Javanese traveling to plantations in Sumatra and the Southeast
L329@P14: Asian mainland, and, in what may have been some of the densest outmigrations ever,
L330@P14: over 300,000 Melanesians and Micronesians who worked on plantations and as seamen
L331@P14: throughout the region.26
L332@P14: Massive internal migration also took place within the major sending regions of
L333@P14: long distance migration. In Europe, migrants from Ireland traveled to England for work,
L334@P14: and from eastern and southern Europe and Belgium to the industrial areas of
L335@P14: northwestern Europe, especially France and Germany. Within Russia, migrants moved
L336@P14: into the growing cities and southern agricultural areas.
L337@P14: 27 Within India they moved to tea
L338@P14: plantations in the south and northeast, to the mines and textile producing regions of
L339@P14: Bengal, and to newly irrigated lands and urban areas throughout the subcontinent.
L340@P14: 28 In
L341@P14: China, they migrated to growing coastal cities, to areas of the Yangtze basin left
L342@P14: underpopulated by the Taiping rebellion, and to borderland areas of the northwest and
L343@P14: southwest, including overland migration to Burma.
L344@P14: 29 Each of these regions hosted at least
L345@P14: 20 million journeys.
L346@P14: Africa experienced net trans-oceanic immigration but at much smaller numbers
L347@P14: than other main destinations and from a wider variety of origins. The immigrants
L348@P14: included over three million French and Italians into north Africa and up to a million other
L349@P14: Europeans, Syrians, Lebanese, Arabs, Indians and Chinese throughout the continent.
L350@P14: 30
L351@P14-15: The end of the transatlantic slave trade led to increased movement of slaves into the16
L352@P15: Western Sudan, Middle East and areas bordering the Indian Ocean in the late 19th
L353@P15: century. Labor migration to plantations and mines in southern and central Africa
L354@P15: increased through the late 19th and twentieth centuries, as did movement to agricultural
L355@P15: areas and coastal cities in western and eastern Africa. Millions of people took part in
L356@P15: these movements, some of whom were coerced or otherwise went to work for European
L357@P15: enterprises, but many of whom also found independent occupations.
L358@P15: 31
L359@P15: The Middle East and ex-Ottoman lands were also at the interstices of the main
L360@P15: long-distance flows described above. Projects such as the Suez Canal and development of
L361@P15: an infrastructure for cotton cultivation in Egypt attracted large amounts of local
L362@P15: migration, while Lebanon and Syria experienced some of the highest overseas emigration
L363@P15: rates in the world. Conflicts surrounding the dissolution of the Ottoman empire also
L364@P15: generated refugee and state fostered migrations that were a foretaste of processes that
L365@P15: would become increasingly common over the twentieth century. By the 1920s, 4 to 6
L366@P15: million people were dislocated in population exchanges between Turkey on the one hand,
L367@P15: and Balkans, Greece and Russia on the other, with Christians moving north and Muslims
L368@P15: moving south. Around a million Armenians were expelled from Turkey to points around
L369@P15: the world, and nearly 400,000 Jews moved to Palestine in the early twentieth century.
L370@P15: 32
L371@P15: Mass movement of refugees would extend to other parts of Europe in the wake of World
L372@P15: War One and the Russian revolution, including the movement of three million Russians,
L373@P15: Poles and Germans out of the Soviet Union. In a different kind of movement, millions of
